items.stem:
Read the following news report from an online news site in Pakistan.

TEENAGERS' APP HELPS RESCUERS REACH FLOOD FAMILIES
A free app built by three students from Lahore has helped rescue teams locate more than 400 families cut off by floods in Sindh province this week.
The app, called Pukaar ("Call"), lets users share their location and needs even with a weak signal.
"We built it in a weekend," said co-founder Hira Baig, 16. "We didn't sleep much."
Rescue coordinator Imran Shah called the app "a lifeline", but warned that thousands of people still have no phone access at all.

Comment on the writer's choice of language in ""a lifeline"".
items.answer: Quotation from an expert: ""a lifeline"" – an authority's metaphor confirms the app's value and makes it vivid.
items.markingKey: Quotation from an expert: ""a lifeline"" – an authority's metaphor confirms the app's value and makes it vivid. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a feature article and hard news.
items.answer: Hard news reports recent events quickly and objectively using the inverted pyramid; a feature explores a topic in depth with description, human interest, quotation and a more personal, reflective style.
items.markingKey: Hard news reports recent events quickly and objectively using the inverted pyramid; a feature explores a topic in depth with description, human interest, quotation and a more personal, reflective style. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following feature article from a weekend newspaper magazine.

The Last Rickshaw Painter of Dhaka
In a workshop no bigger than a parked car, Rafiqul Islam dips a brush thinner than an eyelash into crimson paint. Behind him, a hundred rickshaw panels lean against the wall – film stars, tigers, peacocks, the Taj Mahal.
"Forty years ago there were hundreds of us," he says, without looking up. "Now the machines print stickers. Faster. Cheaper. Dead."
He finishes the tiger's eye. It seems to blink.

How does the writer use the conventions of a feature article to engage readers?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: Instead of a news lead, the feature opens with a descriptive scene ("a workshop no bigger than a parked car") and sensory detail (a brush "thinner than an eyelash"), focusing on one person for human interest. His quotation "Faster. Cheaper. Dead." gives voice and emotion to a wider change, and the closing image of the tiger that "seems to blink" celebrates his craft and leaves a reflective, poignant ending.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Instead of a news lead, the feature opens with a descriptive scene ("a workshop no bigger than a parked car") and sensory detail (a brush "thinner than an eyelash"), focusing on one person for human interest. His quotation "Faster. Cheaper. Dead." gives voice and emotion to a wider change, and the closing image of the tiger that "seems to blink" celebrates his craft and leaves a reflective, poignant ending. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem:
Read the following interview from a teen magazine with a young chef in Lima.

At 16, Valentina Rojas runs a weekend food stall in Lima that sells out in two hours. We asked her how.
Q: Where did you learn to cook?
A: My abuela's kitchen. She never measured anything. She'd say, 'Cook until it smells like home.'
Q: What's the hardest part?
A: Waking up at 4 a.m. to buy fish. And being taken seriously. People ask where my parents are.
Q: Advice for other teens?
A: Start small. Burn things. Try again.

items.stem:
Text A: report of a climate protest (Report A, from a national newspaper).

STUDENTS BRING CITY TO STANDSTILL
Thousands of school pupils skipped lessons on Friday to block the main bridge into the city, causing traffic delays of up to two hours.
Police said three people were arrested for public disorder.
"My son should be in maths, not in the road," said commuter Peter Hale.
Organisers claimed 12,000 attended, though police estimated 5,000.

Text B: report of a climate protest (Report B, from a youth news website).

12,000 YOUNG PEOPLE DEMAND CLIMATE ACTION
Up to 12,000 students marched peacefully across the main bridge on Friday, calling on the government to meet its emissions targets.
"We're missing one day of school. Our future is missing a plan," said organiser Amara Diallo, 16.
Scientists from the city university joined the march.
Police reported three arrests.

Identify ONE similarity and ONE difference between the two texts, supporting each with a reference to both texts.
items.answer: Similarity: both report that a protest took place on the main bridge on Friday and that three people were arrested. Difference: Report A presents the students as disruptive by quoting an annoyed commuter, whereas Report B presents them as peaceful and purposeful by quoting a young organiser.
items.markingKey: Similarity: both report that a protest took place on the main bridge on Friday and that three people were arrested. Difference: Report A presents the students as disruptive by quoting an annoyed commuter, whereas Report B presents them as peaceful and purposeful by quoting a young organiser. One mark for each valid, supported point; credit other valid comparisons.

items.stem: List three choices that make Report A represent the protest negatively.

Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling. Comparison must be sustained across both texts (criterion B).

Write the opening of a feature article (about 250 words) about a person in your community who keeps a tradition alive.
items.answer: Indicative content: a descriptive opening scene; human-interest focus; sensory detail; direct quotation; background context; a reflective ending; headline.

items.stem: Interview a family member or friend about a significant experience and write it up as a feature (about 400 words) with an introduction and quotations.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "representation".
items.answer: The way the media presents people, groups or events, which constructs a version of reality
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the way the media presents people, groups or events, which constructs a version of reality. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "feature article".
items.answer: A longer article exploring a topic, person or trend in depth, using description, human interest and a personal style
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a longer article exploring a topic, person or trend in depth, using description, human interest and a personal style. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why follow-up questions are important in an interview.
items.answer: They explore interesting answers more deeply and show active listening, producing richer material.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They explore interesting answers more deeply and show active listening, producing richer material. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between representation and reality.
items.answer: Reality is the event itself; representation is a constructed version shaped by selection, framing and language. Every report is a representation.
items.markingKey: Reality is the event itself; representation is a constructed version shaped by selection, framing and language. Every report is a representation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between hard news and a feature article.
items.answer: Hard news reports recent events quickly and objectively using the inverted pyramid; a feature explores a topic in depth with description, human interest, quotation and a more personal, reflective style.
items.markingKey: Hard news reports recent events quickly and objectively using the inverted pyramid; a feature explores a topic in depth with description, human interest, quotation and a more personal, reflective style. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following interview from a teen magazine with a young chef in Lima.

At 16, Valentina Rojas runs a weekend food stall in Lima that sells out in two hours. We asked her how.
Q: Where did you learn to cook?
A: My abuela's kitchen. She never measured anything. She'd say, 'Cook until it smells like home.'
Q: What's the hardest part?
A: Waking up at 4 a.m. to buy fish. And being taken seriously. People ask where my parents are.
Q: Advice for other teens?
A: Start small. Burn things. Try again.

Explain how the introduction in the magazine's voice contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: The introduction in the magazine's voice: it frames the interview and explains why readers should care.
items.markingKey: The introduction in the magazine's voice: it frames the interview and explains why readers should care. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: "Youth news sites are always more biased than national newspapers." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Any outlet can be biased; readers should analyse each report's selection, framing and language.
items.markingKey: Any outlet can be biased; readers should analyse each report's selection, framing and language. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following news report from a coastal newspaper in Kenya.

RECORD TURTLE HATCHING ON WATAMU BEACH
More than 1,200 green turtle hatchlings reached the sea from Watamu Beach on Saturday night, the highest number recorded in a single night since monitoring began in 1998.
Volunteers from Local Ocean Conservation guarded 14 nests for eight weeks.
"We were on our knees in the sand at 2 a.m., counting," said volunteer Amani Mwangi, 17. "Every single one made it past the crabs."
Experts warn that rising sand temperatures could reduce numbers in future years.

Analyse how the phrase "1,200 ... 14 nests for eight weeks" helps the writer achieve their purpose.
items.answer: Precise figures: "1,200 ... 14 nests for eight weeks" – numbers make the report factual and credible.
items.markingKey: Precise figures: "1,200 ... 14 nests for eight weeks" – numbers make the report factual and credible. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Bias in the news is unavoidable, so readers should not worry about it."
items.answer: Some bias is unavoidable, which is exactly why readers should compare sources and analyse framing.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: all reporting involves selection; perfect neutrality is impossible. Arguments against: some reports are far more balanced than others; bias can mislead and polarise. Supported judgement: Some bias is unavoidable, which is exactly why readers should compare sources and analyse framing.

items.stem: "Feature articles are more valuable than hard news." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Both are valuable for different purposes: hard news informs quickly, features deepen understanding.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they give depth and context; they build empathy. Arguments against: hard news informs quickly about urgent events; features can be subjective. Supported judgement: Both are valuable for different purposes: hard news informs quickly, features deepen understanding. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: "The interviewer is as important as the interviewee." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The interviewer shapes the interview through questions and editing, but should foreground the interviewee's voice.
